newsitem.title: UK: LME welcomes SIB review, will implement changes.
newsitem.headline: LME welcomes SIB review, will implement changes.

text.p: The London Metal Exchange (LME) welcomes the result of the wide-ranging review of the metals market carried out by the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) and will introduce many of the recommended changes.
"As we anticipated, the SIB review on the whole fully endorses our modus operandi," LME Chief Executive David King said.

"We will implement many of them (changes) over an agreed period of time once the issues have had a public airing and we have had an opportunity to discuss them with our members and their clients," he said. The SIB, Britain's top regulator, was asked by the LME to carry out a top-to-bottom review of the LME after the Sumitomo scandal shocked world metal markets in June.

In mid-June, Sumitomo Corp of Japan fired its head copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka, alleging he had admitted running up losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trading. The SIB sent out a consultative document to market participants, seeking views from the LME's users over the Exchange's practices. It also looked at the LME's governance, resources and regulatory effectiveness.
"The respondents (to the review) have said they are content with the way we operate and SIB has said they see no systemic risk arising from the way we operate," King said.
In the review, published today, SIB recommended that the LME review its rules concerning historic price carries, member/customer relationships and non-regulated customers.

It also said the LME should examine warehousing, price transparancy of futures, options, and stocks, and consider the composition of the Board, the various committees and the role and structure of the Executive. The areas that the SIB looked at and gave a clean bill-of-health to are being retained.

"Non-cash clearing, giving of credit, non-segregation of funds go hand-in-hand. There was an endorsement by market users that they are comfortable with those processes, and no will for them to be changed."
"SIB has not identified any systemic risk issues arising from those," King said.

"Overall the SIB document gives its and the industry's imprimatur on our methods of trading. We should not lose sight of the fact that this review was undertaken at our request against the background of the Sumitomo affair," King added.

The LME is keen to seek ways to minimise the probability of such an event re-occuring, and one route is to strengthen its rules in terms of information and jurisdiction over members and their clients.

"However, we have to strike the right balance and it will be wrong to assume that we would arrogate to ourselves the right to have access to large tranches of physical OTC (over-the-counter) business," he said.
The LME indicated at the time the review was commissioned, and subsequently at October's annual LME dinner that there were areas that could be enhanced.

"We recognised the interest of market-users to seek more information and had commenced a series of dialogues with market-users in order to identify more specifically what they would seek in terms of enhanced transparency," King said.
The SIB document is opaque, although the main areas cover enhanced transparency, market monitoring, increased resources and a review of the the LME's governing structure.
So the LME will seek feedback from its members and have a thorough debate before changes are implemented.
"We are, however, willing and keen to change in certain areas. In the last few years we have made many changes of our own volition," he said.
The Sumitomo affair and the SIB review had perhaps hastened the process of change at the LME in some of the areas.

"Many people are resistant to change. One needs a catalyst to tip the scales. From the Exchange's point of view we had an extensive "to-do' list, and some of the items have now moved to the top of the pile," King added.
The LME was going to strengthen its rulebook under its own volition, and the SIB welcomed the Exchange's initiative in planning this, he said.

"Our recommendations will enhance the standards of market integrity delivered by the LME, without attempting to make members and users adopt practices more suited to other markets meeting different user needs," David Pritchard, an SIB official who led the review, said in a statement.

The SIB said more transparency was needed and proposed the exchange release more information on inter-office trading, options and inventory data. The LME should consider moving to an electronic system for warrants, but costs had to be considered.

The LME should reorganise its board to avoid potential conflicts of interest, separating regulatory and commercial functions, the SIB review said. The chief executive needed to be strengthened and a new market regulation post should be created. The exchange will propose a timetable for acting on the recommendations by January 16.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8065
